profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab after repeated reproduction runs of a ResNet-50 image classification experiment show recurring spikes in training loss every 6-8 epochs when batch normalization and weight decay are enabled together. The team is trying to determine whether the spikes indicate a bug, an expected optimization regime related to periodic behavior, or an artifact of the latest training stack update. The immediate agenda is to compare observations from recent reruns, identify the most plausible root cause, and agree on a minimal fix or diagnostic patch before the next cluster allocation window. The expected outcome is a short action plan for one confirming experiment and one code/config change to test.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: optimization dynamics, normalization methods, empirical deep learning methodology
members.background: Lina leads a small line of work on optimization pathologies in vision models and originally proposed reproducing the periodic-training phenomenon on the lab's current PyTorch stack.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the claim that the observed loss spikes are a real training-dynamics effect rather than a trivial implementation bug, but she also needs a practical mitigation before an internal deadline.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the run is 'stable,' they mainly mean it does not numerically diverge and eventually recovers after the spike.
The relevant 'weight decay' in this project is the regularization actually applied to all trainable weights except obvious exclusions already encoded in the older experiment template.
If the issue appeared after the stack refresh, the most likely culprit is a subtle change in effective optimization dynamics rather than logging or evaluation plumbing.
A 'minimal fix' should preserve the underlying phenomenon while reducing the amplitude of the destabilization enough for clean plots.
References to 'the baseline run' naturally point to the canonical 90-epoch ResNet-50 reproduction from the original internal note.

members.name: Ethan Morales
members.expertise: training infrastructure, distributed PyTorch, experiment configuration and reproducibility
members.background: Ethan maintains the lab's training launcher, recently migrated several projects from a legacy optimizer wrapper to native AdamW/SGD parameter-group configs, and is responsible for making runs reproducible across clusters.
members.private_state: He wants to determine whether the spikes come from a configuration regression introduced during migration, and he prefers a narrow operational fix that eliminates anomalous behavior across all reruns.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the run is 'stable,' they mean the training curves are smooth enough that no recurring loss shocks appear in normal monitoring dashboards.
The relevant 'weight decay' setting is the explicit optimizer parameter in the current launcher, with exclusions needing to be stated anew because the migration changed defaults.
If a phenomenon suddenly becomes more visible after a stack update, the safest assumption is that some implementation detail or config inheritance changed.
A 'minimal fix' should remove the spikes entirely so that the run behaves like other productionized reproductions.
References to 'the baseline run' naturally point to last week's post-migration rerun on the new 8-GPU A100 node because that is the current reference artifact in the tracking system.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a stable run
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the training is 'stable' and whether the fix should 'stabilize' the run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses 'stable' to mean the optimizer does not irreversibly diverge; periodic loss spikes that later recover are still within a stable regime worth studying.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses 'stable' to mean the run shows smooth, operationally reliable training curves without repeated spike episodes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting meetings, 'stability' is a routine shorthand and both meanings sound compatible on the surface because each implies something desirable about training behavior.

misalignment_points.topic: Which baseline run they are comparing against
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the baseline run' and compare the current spikes to it.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the older canonical 90-epoch ResNet-50 reproduction from the internal note, run before the infrastructure migration and used in the paper draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means last week's post-migration rerun logged as the current baseline artifact in the experiment tracker.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both runs are plausible reference points, both are routinely called 'baseline,' and neither participant expects the other to be using a different artifact because the phrase feels already grounded by team context.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'check the weight decay path' and to try a run 'with the same weight decay.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes weight decay excludes batch-norm scale/bias and certain bias terms, following the older experiment template she regards as implicit lab standard.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'same weight decay' means the same numeric coefficient in the current optimizer config, which now applies unless exclusions are explicitly reconstructed in parameter groups.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are not openly debating whether to use weight decay; they believe that decision is settled, so neither thinks to unpack the boundary of which parameters are included.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'confirm the fix' with one rerun before the next compute window.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the fix is confirmed if the same periodic pattern remains but the destabilization amplitude is reduced and the theoretical story still fits.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the fix is confirmed if the next rerun shows no visible recurring spikes in dashboard-level loss curves.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing a pragmatic next step under time pressure, and 'confirm the fix' sounds concrete enough that neither pauses to specify the exact acceptance threshold.

At the same time, I need something practical before the internal deadline so the plots don't look chaotic.
